newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: HOLD THE FAT ON CZECH MILO, TRIM SETUZA - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: HOLD THE FAT ON CZECH MILO, TRIM SETUZA - ANALYSTS.

text.p: Of the two largest companies in the popular Czech fats and oils industry, analysts said the share price of Setuza a.s. was overly plump while Milo a.s. had some room to gain.
Both companies make vegetable oils and margarines for calorie-demanding Czech kitchens along with cosmetics and soap.
But analysts said Setuza has been deficient in marketing and advertising and was loosing the battle of the bulge.
"Setuza hasn't enough means for agressive advertisement," said Tomas Navratil of Akro Capital in Prague.
A survey of Prague analysts showed Setuza's share prices to be more reasonable at 1,500 crowns, not the 2,320 crowns where it closed on Friday, down 35.
Setuza, based in the northern Czech city of Usti nad Labem, had sales of 4.03 billion crowns in 1995, but analysts said 1996 sales would be flat despite a growing Czech economy.
First-half gross profit at Setuza was up 72 million crowns to 186 million, but full-year net is not expected to surpass last year's result of 94 million crowns.

"It's expected that by the end of the year there will be a marked jump in the cost of rape seed, which grew poorly this year," said Marcela Gronychova of OFT Brokers, citing a key raw material in many Setuza products.

Meanwhile analysts said Milo, based in the eastern city of Olomouc, was modernising production, with capable management, and a fine long-term strategy. The company has been building solid profits and sales since 1993, they said.
Jana Tuckova of Patria Finance said Milo's strong connections with cross-town drink bottler Seliko a.s. allows for cooperative marketing and distribution, thus cutting costs.
The leaner, meaner Milo had 1995 net profit of 139 million crowns on sales of 2.88 billion crowns. All profits were ploughed back into the company last year.
However this year's net is expected to fall to between 110 to 125 million crowns because of higher indebtedness tied to investment and rising raw materials costs.
Still, analysts said Milo's share price -- down 20 at 1,540 on the Prague Stock Exchange on Friday -- was attractive up to around 1,700 crowns.
Some analysts advised however to hold Milo shares or resist buying until the results of a recent takeover battle are clearer.
They said a group combining Emgrup a.s. and an agriculture and forestry fund had recently built a majority stake despite heavy pressure from the IPB Group led by Investicni a Postovni Banka .
